lesson_title: Day 6 Daily Quiz: Review of Day 5 (the Tron lab: deposit addresses, Energy and an issuer freeze)

lectures.title: Tron lab: sweeps, Energy and the USDT blacklist

questions.question_stem: In the Tron lab's worked example, a deposit address sweeps its whole USDT balance to one wallet, and each sweep burns 13.3959 TRX for Energy. Who supplied that TRX?
questions.correct_answer: A separate account sent the TRX to the deposit address 10 to 15 minutes before each sweep.
incorrect_answers: The depositor, who attached the TRX to the same transfer that brought the USDT to the address.
The receiving wallet, which paid the sweep from its own balance when the USDT arrived there.
Nobody, because a sweep that moves a whole balance is free of any Energy charge on Tron.
questions.explanation: The sweep itself cost Energy, and the address had none, so it burned the TRX it held. A third account, not the depositor and not the receiver, topped the address up before each sweep (624, 864 and 894 seconds ahead). That outside payer is part of the deposit-address pattern.

questions.question_stem: A second Tron address makes 13 whole-balance sweeps, each using 64,285 Energy and burning 0 TRX, the Energy delegated from another account. Compared with the worked example, what does that show?
questions.correct_answer: Someone lent it Energy by staking TRX behind it, so a third party still pays for the sweeps.
incorrect_answers: The address owner staked their own TRX, so the owner and the sweep target are one party.
The sweeps were free because the balances were small, so no one paid anything for them.
The sweeps did not happen, because a transfer that burns no TRX is not recorded on Tron.
questions.explanation: In the worked example a payer sent TRX and the sweep burned it. Here the payer lent Energy, so nothing is burned. Either way, someone other than the address pays for its sweeps. Nothing in the record says who controls the lender's TRX either.

questions.question_stem: That second address was funded by 12 senders and swept to one address that no published source names. What confidence fits calling it a custodial deposit address?
questions.correct_answer: Moderate at most, and more often Low, because the pattern fits but no source ties the destination to a service.
incorrect_answers: High, because the sweeps match the worked example's pattern, which was already shown to be a deposit address there too.
None can be given, because the chain holds no evidence of any kind about how an address behaves or who pays for it.
Moderate, because 12 separate senders count as 12 independent kinds of evidence for the one same service they use.
questions.explanation: Many senders, whole-balance sweeps to one address and a third party paying each sweep repeat the worked example. Nothing names the destination, so the label is a pattern only. The 12 senders are one kind of evidence, repeated; High needs independent kinds.

questions.question_stem: The Tron lab shows two wallets blacklisted by the USDT contract. Which detail must a sentence about their current status carry?
questions.correct_answer: The block and time of the read, because the contract answers for the present only and a later read could differ.
incorrect_answers: The name of each wallet's owner, because the contract stores it beside each blacklist entry that it holds.
The date of the freeze alone, because a wallet that is blacklisted stays blacklisted for good once the issuer adds it.
The fee paid for the freeze, because it shows which agency asked the issuer to act on those two wallets.
questions.explanation: The AddedBlackList events are fixed on the chain (block 82,092,618, 23 Apr 2026), but whether a wallet is still blacklisted, and its balance, is read from the contract at a moment. The lab states both as of block 87,600,650. Who owns the wallets and why comes from sources, not from the chain.
